title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
The Local and Global Dynamics of Valenced Networks



Relationships are not just present or absent; they carry emotional valence.
Balance Theory is the foundational framework linking:

Local, psychological micro-motives.
Global, macro-structural network patterns (like polarization).

Today we will cover: Dyadic Balance, Signed Graphs, Triadic Balance, Structural Balance, and Clusterability.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Anatomy of Sentiment Networks



Valenced ties are links representing positive (\(+\)) or negative (\(-\)) feelings, evaluations, or behaviors.

Positive valence: Liking, helping, admiring, loving.
Negative valence: Hating, bullying, fighting, distrusting.

A signed graph features a set of vertices \(V\) and two disjoint sets of edges:

Positive links (\(E^+\)) and negative links (\(E^-\)).

These networks represent stable social attitudes rather than fleeting events.
We can represent them with a signed adjacency matrix: \(+1\) for positive ties, \(-1\) for negative ties, \(0\) for no tie.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Fritz Heider’s Dyadic Balance



Developed by social psychologist Fritz Heider (1946) to examine how ties cohere within a single pair.
Distinction between:

Symmetric ties: Relations implied by similarity or co-membership (e.g., sharing a workspace).
Asymmetric ties: Directional sentiments (e.g., liking).

First Proposition: Similarity breeds liking. Sharing co-membership or space breeds positive asymmetric ties (\(aSb \implies aLb\)).
Forms a positive feedback loop: We spend more time with those we like (\(aLb \implies aSb\)).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Proximity, Similarity, and Multiplexity



Over time, people accumulate multiple types of ties, leading to multiplex ties (“multistranded” connections).
Principle of Propinquity (Newcomb 1956): Sharing physical space or social contexts automatically facilitates acquaintance and liking.

Proximity breeds interaction, which breeds similarity, which in turn breeds liking, support, and advice.

Relationships transition from uniplex (single-stranded) to multiplex.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Dyadic Balance and Cognitive Tension



Second Proposition: We strive to maintain positive asymmetric ties with those we are similar to.
Situations where similarity is paired with dislike (\(aSb \land aDb\)) are unbalanced.

Creates cognitive inconsistency and an unpleasant state of affective tension (e.g., hating a forced co-worker).

Resolution of Imbalance:

Break the similarity tie (e.g., quit the job).
Transform the dislike into liking (e.g., adapt to like the co-worker).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Fritz Heider’s P-O-Q Triad



To analyze triads, Heider extended dyadic balance to three distinct elements: the P-O-Q Triad.
Person (P): The focal individual from whose cognitive perspective the triad is analyzed.
Other (O): Towards whom P holds a directed sentiment.
Third Party / Object (Q): Another actor, group, organization, or abstract cultural idea.
Sentiments are modeled via directed, signed edges (\(+\) or \(-\)) going from P to O, P to Q, and O to Q.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Mathematics of Triadic Balance



A triad is balanced if the product of its three edge signs is positive: \[\text{Sign}(P, O) \times \text{Sign}(O, Q) \times \text{Sign}(P, Q) = +1\]
Simplified Identification Rule: A triad is balanced if it has an even number of negative links (exactly zero or two).
Balanced configurations are stable and represent harmonious sentiments, creating no cognitive tension.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balanced Triads: The 4 Stable Configurations




“A friend of a friend is a friend” (\(+ \times + \times + = +1\))

Example: You (P) and friend (O) both like the same classmate (Q).

“An enemy of an enemy is a friend” (\(- \times - \times + = +1\))

Example: You (P) and ally (Q) form a bond against a mutual rival (O).

“A friend of an enemy is an enemy” (\(- \times + \times - = +1\))

Example: Your rival (O) has a close friend (Q); you start to dislike Q.

“An enemy of a friend is an enemy” (\(+ \times - \times - = +1\))

Example: Your country ally (O) declares war on country (Q); you also oppose Q.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Unbalanced Triads: The 4 Unstable Configurations




“A friend of my friend is my enemy” (\(+ \times + \times - = -1\))

Example: Friend (O) likes (Q), whom you (P) dislike.

“An enemy of a friend is a friend” (\(+ \times - \times + = -1\))

Example: Partner (O) hates Marvel movies (Q), which you (P) love.

“A friend of an enemy is a friend” (\(- \times + \times + = -1\))

Example: You (P) and your rival (O) are both attracted to the same person (Q).

“An enemy of my enemy is also my enemy” (\(- \times - \times - = -1\))

Example: You (P) dislike both the Yankees (O) and Red Sox (Q).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Tension and Change



The basic idea is that unbalanced configurations will tend to transition to balanced configurations.
Unbalanced configurations produce tension in P, leading them to change their sentiments toward O or Q to generate balance.
Balanced configurations are stable equilibrium states.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Cross-Pressure



Because we have multiple social relations, we are sometimes caught between worlds.
This is called cross-pressure.
Example: having two friends with different attitudes towards the same object.
Balance theory predicts that P will have an ambivalent attitude toward the object.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Cross-Pressure in Real-Life: Politics



Political preferences provide a classic illustration of cross-pressure.
Imagine you (P) have a brother (O1) who is a passionate Democrat (\(+\)) and a sister (O2) who strongly opposes them (\(-\)).
Because you have positive bonds with both, you find yourself cross-pressured regarding the Democrats (Q).
This pressure produces social ambivalence, often leading individuals to identify as moderates or independents with no strong partisan affiliation.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Structural Balance at the Network Level
text:
Structural Balance at the Network Level



Balance theory can be scaled up from individual cognitive triads to the whole network level.
This extension is known as Structural Balance Theory.
In its original formulation, it applies to complete signed graphs, where every pair of actors is connected by either a positive or negative link.
In a signed adjacency matrix representation of a signed graph:

Positive links are represented by \(+1\).
Negative links are represented by \(-1\).
Non-adjacent nodes are represented by \(0\).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: The Fundamental Theorem of Structural Balance
text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Structural Balance



The fundamental theorem of structural balance was discovered by the mathematicians Dorwin Cartwright and Frank Harary in 1956.
It states that when a graph is balanced, it can be split into two groups such that there are:

Only positive links within groups.
Only negative links between groups.

Balance is not necessarily good! Structural balance is equivalent to perfect group polarization.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Signed Matrices & Faction Detection



How can we mathematically recover and identify factions in a balanced network?
Rearrange the rows and columns of the signed adjacency matrix such that nodes in the same faction are adjacent.
This permutation yields a block-diagonal signed matrix.
Inside the diagonal blocks, cells are \(+1\) (internal cohesion), whereas off-diagonal blocks are entirely \(-1\) (external conflict).
The 3 × 3 blocks below mirror the two three-person factions in the previous slide’s graph.


Faction Block-Diagonal Matrix
\[M = \begin{pmatrix}
  \begin{array}{ccc|ccc}
    \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\
    \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\
    \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\ \hline
    - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \\
    - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \\
    - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+}
  \end{array}
\end{pmatrix}\]

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Cycles and Paths in Balanced Graphs
text:
Cycles and Paths in Balanced Graphs



Partitioning has direct, rigid consequences for paths and cycles in complete graphs:
Cycles: All cycles in a balanced signed graph must have a positive sign product.

Staying inside a group uses only positive links.
Spanning across groups requires crossing the boundary an even number of times, multiplying an even number of negative signs to yield a positive product.

Paths:

Paths ending in the same group have a positive product.
Paths ending in different groups have a negative product (due to odd boundary crossings).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Checking for Balance with Matrix Powers
text:
Checking for Balance with Matrix Powers



How can we test balance in a large network without drawing every cycle?
Raise the signed adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) to the \(p\)-th power.
Each diagonal entry \(a_{ii}^{(p)}\) sums the sign products of all closed walks of length \(p\) starting and ending at node \(i\).
The test: If the graph is balanced, every diagonal entry of \(\mathbf{A}^p\) is non-negative for all \(p\) up to the number of nodes.
A single negative diagonal entry reveals a negative cycle of length \(p\) — and the graph is unbalanced.


The test in symbols
\[a_{ii}^{(p)} \geq 0 \; \text{for all } i,\; p = 1, \dots, g\]
If any entry is negative:
\[a_{ii}^{(p)} < 0 \implies \text{unbalanced cycle}\]

No need to enumerate cycles — the matrix does the counting.
A practical check for real, messy networks.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Measuring Partial Balance



Real networks are almost never perfectly balanced, so we measure the degree of balance.
Cycle Index of Balance: the share of all cycles whose sign product is positive. \[\text{Cycle Index} = \frac{PC}{TC}\]
Ranges from 0 (completely unbalanced) to 1 (perfectly balanced).
Line Index of Balance (Harary 1959): the minimum number of edge signs that must be flipped to make the graph perfectly balanced.



A large network with a Line Index of 1 or 2 is extremely close to complete balance.
Even when cycle-counting finds dozens of unbalanced cycles, a small Line Index says the polarized structure is nearly there.
Short cycles matter more psychologically, so weighted versions (Henley, Horsfall & De Soto 1969) give triads extra weight.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Directed Balance: Semicycles



Real sentiment ties are often asymmetric — you like someone who dislikes you.
Restricting balance to strict directed cycles (arrows all pointing the same way) would miss most tension: Your friend Alex dislikes Jordan, yet you like both. No directed cycle exists, but the tension is real.
Semipath: a path that ignores arrow direction.
Semicycle: a closed semipath (a cycle in the underlying undirected graph).
A signed digraph is balanced if and only if every semicycle has a positive sign (an even number of negative arcs).



The Cartwright–Harary partition rule carries over unchanged: positive arcs within factions, negative arcs between them.
One rule-violating positive tie across factions injects unbalanced semicycles into the whole network.
This is the directed version of everything we just did with cycles.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Empirical Case Study: Political Blogs



Balanced states describe stable polarization and conflict, not harmony.
Adamic & Glance (2005) examined the hyperlink network of 2004-election political bloggers.
Two highly connected factions (Liberals, Conservatives); dense internal linking, sparse cross-group linking — an echo chamber.
The hyperlink data are unsigned; the figure’s negative ties illustrate the predicted structure, not measured hostility.
Balance explains why polarized factions are stable — and a balanced state need not be a “good” one.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Beyond Two Factions: Davis’s Theorem



Cartwright & Harary’s model splits networks into exactly two opposing factions.
This is too restrictive for many real-world networks, such as school cliques, gangs, or multi-party politics.
In 1967, sociologist James Davis introduced his Clusterability Theorem.
He generalized structural balance so that a network could fragment into any number of distinct clusters (\(k \ge 1\)), rather than just two.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The All-Negative Triad Rule



Classical balance considers a triad with three negative ties (everyone hating everyone else) to be unbalanced.
Davis argued that in highly factionalized contexts, it is perfectly stable for three individuals from completely different, competing groups to dislike one another.
The Clustering Criterion (Davis 1967): A graph is clusterable if and only if it contains no cycle of any length with exactly one negative tie.
For complete graphs this reduces to a triad test: no triad with exactly one negative tie. All-positive, two-negative, and all-negative triads are all permitted.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Ranked Clusterability: Bridging Balance and Hierarchy
text:
Ranked Clusterability: Bridging Balance and Hierarchy



Balance and clusterability both assume horizontal, symmetric sentiment structures.
Real groups often have vertical hierarchies — status, dominance, prestige.
Ranked Clusterability (Davis & Leinhardt 1972): clusters that are themselves hierarchically ordered.

Within clusters: horizontal, positive ties (peer solidarity).
Between clusters: vertical ties. Positive ties point up the hierarchy (deference); negative or null ties point down or across unranked clusters.

This is the mathematical bridge from balance theory to status and dominance hierarchies.



Think of an office: peers are mutual friends, everyone looks up to the executives, discipline flows downward.
Same local logic (no odd cycles of negativity), but the factions are now stacked, not side by side.
Coming up next: theories of valenced interactions, including dominance hierarchies in detail.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Summary: Structural Balance vs. Clusterability



Structural Balance (Cartwright-Harary 1956):

Local rule: Triads cannot have an odd number of negative ties.
Global topology: Splits the network into exactly two factions.

Clusterability (Davis 1967):

Local rule: Relaxes constraints by permitting all-negative triads (no triads with exactly one negative tie).
Global topology: Splits the network into any number of clusters (\(k \ge 1\)).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Dyadic Balance: From Similarities to Interactions
text:
Dyadic Balance: From Similarities to Interactions

Ideas of dyadic balance were first described in a famous paper written by Fritz Heider in 1946.
Ties differ based on whether they are based on:

Similarities.
Interactions.

The basic principle is that people seek balance between similarities and interactions.

People tend to interact with people who are similar to them.

If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two people, \(S\) is a tie based on similarity and \(R\) is a tie based on interaction:

\[\alpha S \beta \rightarrow \alpha R \beta\]

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Dyadic Balance: Reading the Principle

\(\alpha S \beta \rightarrow \alpha R \beta\) reads: “A tie of type \(S\) between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) leads to a tie of type \(R\) between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).”
This applies to every combination of similarities and interactions.
Examples:

People tend to like the people they spend time with.
People tend to help people who belong to the same groups as them.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: What Counts as Similarities and Interactions?
text:
What Counts as Similarities and Interactions?



Similarities

Propinquity (same place).
Homophily (same social category).
Co-memberships (same social groups).




Interactions

Communicating with.
Liking.
Helping.




Reference: Borgatti, S. P., Mehra, A., Brass, D. J., & Labianca, G. (2009). Network analysis in the social sciences. Science, 323(5916), 892–895.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Worked Example: Spending Time and Liking
text:
Worked Example: Spending Time and Liking



Balanced: Simbi and Keryl spend time together and like each other.

Similarity and interaction point the same way.

Unbalanced: Simbi and Keryl spend time together, but the liking is one-sided.

A similarity paired with a missing or hostile interaction creates tension.

Balance theory predicts the tension gets resolved: the liking becomes mutual, or the time spent together dries up.












Solid green: liking (directed). Blue: spend time with (symmetric).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Worked Example: Same Groups and Helping
text:
Worked Example: Same Groups and Helping



Balanced: Simbi and Keryl belong to the same groups and help each other.
Unbalanced: They share group memberships, but the helping only flows one way.
Same logic, different content: any symmetric similarity tie wants to be matched by reciprocal interaction ties.












Solid green: help (directed). Blue: same group (symmetric).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: The Cycle Runs Both Ways: From Interactions to Similarities
text:
The Cycle Runs Both Ways: From Interactions to Similarities

After the first cycle of similarities leading to interactions, interactions can lead to further similarities: \(\alpha R \beta \rightarrow \alpha S \beta\).
People tend to think like (share the opinions and attitudes of) the people they interact with.
People tend to adopt the same tastes and fashions as the people in the same organizations as them.
People tend to spend time with the people they like.
Similarities and interactions feed each other in a continuing loop.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Signed Graphs



Signed graphs are a special kind of graph featuring:

One set of vertices \(V\).
Two disjoint sets of edges:

Positive links (\(E^+\)).
Negative links (\(E^-\)).


The graph is written \(G = \{V, E^+, E^-\}\).
Two sets are disjoint when they don’t share any members (their intersection is the empty set \(\emptyset\)).
Signed graphs can be either directed or undirected.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balance Theory

Balance theory is a social psychological theory designed to explain expected triadic configurations in sentiment networks.
Sentiment networks are built from valenced ties (e.g., positive or negative).
There are four building blocks in balance theory.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 1: A Person (P)



The person (P).
We “look” at the triad from this person’s point of view.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 2: An Object (O)



An object (O) towards which the focal person has some kind of sentiment.
The sentiment can be positive or negative.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 3: A Third Party (Q)



A third party (Q) towards which both the person and the other also have some kind of sentiment.
Q does not have to be a real person! It could be any object.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 4: Directed Signed Edges



A set of directed signed edges indicating positive (solid green) or negative (dashed red) sentiments:

From P to O.
From P to Q.
From O to Q.

This configuration reads: Person (P) likes Other (O); Other (O) likes the third party (Q); but Person (P) dislikes the third party.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Triad in Everyday Terms












Sounds dicey!
You (P) have a friend (O) who likes another classmate (Q) whom you dislike.












Everything’s fine!
You (P) have a friend (O) who likes another classmate (Q) whom you also like.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Triad in Everyday Terms (continued)












Seems fine?
You (P) have an enemy (O) who likes another classmate (Q) whom you also dislike.












Trouble in paradise!
You (P) love Marvel movies (Q), but your long-time partner O (whom you like, duh!) hates them.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Eight Configurations

There are eight (8) configurations, featuring one-way directed links from:

Person (P) to Other (O).
Person (P) to Third Party (Q).
Other (O) to Third Party (Q).

Four of them are balanced; four are unbalanced.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balanced Configurations













In each balanced configuration, the sentiments cohere.
“A friend of a friend is a friend.”
“An enemy of an enemy is a friend.”
“A friend of an enemy is an enemy.”
“An enemy of a friend is an enemy.”

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Unbalanced Configurations













In each unbalanced configuration, the sentiments collide.
“A friend of my friend is my enemy.”
“An enemy of a friend is a friend.”
“A friend of an enemy is a friend.”
“An enemy of my enemy is also my enemy.”

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Mathematics of Balance Theory

Remember the rules of sign multiplication from basic algebra?

\[+1 \times +1 = +1 \qquad +1 \times -1 = -1 \qquad -1 \times -1 = +1\]

They apply to balance theory!

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Unbalanced Triads Have a Negative Product
text:
Unbalanced Triads Have a Negative Product

If you multiply the signs of the edges of each unbalanced triad, you get a negative number. Try it!
\((+1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)
\((+1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)
\((-1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)
\((-1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Balanced Triads Have a Positive Product
text:
Balanced Triads Have a Positive Product

Conversely, if you multiply the signs of the edges of each balanced triad, you get a positive number.
\((-1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)
\((+1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)
\((-1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)
\((+1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: A Link Between Mathematics and the Logic of Social Relations
text:
A Link Between Mathematics and the Logic of Social Relations

“A friend of a friend is a friend”: \(+1_{PO} \times +1_{OQ} \times +1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
“An enemy of an enemy is a friend”: \(-1_{PO} \times -1_{OQ} \times +1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
“A friend of an enemy is an enemy”: \(-1_{PO} \times +1_{OQ} \times -1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
“An enemy of a friend is an enemy”: \(+1_{PO} \times -1_{OQ} \times -1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
Every folk rule for balanced sentiment is a sign product equal to \(+1\).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Resolving Cross-Pressure



To achieve balance and remove the ambivalence, P can:

Change their own attitude toward Friend 1 or Friend 2.
Convince either Friend 1 or Friend 2 to change their attitude toward the object.

The same tension-and-resolution logic that works triad by triad also works for whole networks. That is where we go next.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: From Triadic Balance to Structural Balance
text:
From Triadic Balance to Structural Balance

If a triad is balanced, then it is so from every member’s point of view.
We just need to change the interpretation!
Take this balanced triad and rotate the “you” position around the triangle.
From the bottom node: “a friend of an enemy is an enemy.”
From the lower-right node: “an enemy of an enemy is a friend.”
From the top node: “an enemy of a friend is an enemy.”

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Balance as a Triad-Level Property, Regardless of Perspective
text:
Balance as a Triad-Level Property, Regardless of Perspective













This means we can define balance as a triad-level property regardless of “perspective.”
For node A: “friends of enemies are enemies.”
For nodes B and C: “enemies of friends are enemies.”
The triad is balanced for everyone!

A Signed Graph with Named Edge Sets

The graph is \(G = \{V, E^+, E^-\}\).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Structural Balance Applies to Complete Signed Graphs
text:
Structural Balance Applies to Complete Signed Graphs



Structural Balance Theory applies to complete signed graphs.
A complete signed graph is a graph in which every node is connected to every other by either a positive line or a negative line.
No zeros anywhere off the diagonal.

Every off-diagonal cell is filled: \(+1\) within each group, \(-1\) between the groups.
Every one of the \(\binom{6}{3} = 20\) triples is a triad we can check.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balance as a Whole-Network Property

When a whole signed graph only contains balanced triads, then the graph is also balanced.
Balance can be a whole-network property!
A signed graph in which every triple is balanced is called a balanced signed graph.
Checking twenty triads by hand sounds tedious — there is a shortcut.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Triad-Checking Shortcut

Trick: a triad is balanced if it has either zero or two negative links.
A triad is unbalanced if the number of negative links is odd (one or three).
This follows directly from sign multiplication: the product of the edge signs is positive exactly when an even number of them is negative.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Checking the Complete Graph, Triad by Triad
text:
Checking the Complete Graph, Triad by Triad













ABF triad: three positive links. Balanced!
ABC triad: one positive (A–B), two negative. Balanced!
CDF triad: C–D positive, C–F and D–F negative. Balanced!
BEF triad: B–F positive, B–E and E–F negative. Balanced!
ACE triad: A–C and A–E negative, C–E positive. Balanced!
And so on for all the triads. Every one checks out.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Structural Balance in Everyday Life



P (a liberal retweeter), O (a liberal tweeter), Q (a liberal tweet):

All sentiments positive. A balanced triad.

P (a conservative retweeter), O (a conservative tweeter), Q (a conservative tweet):

Also all positive. Another balanced triad.




P (a liberal retweeter), O (a conservative tweeter), Q (a conservative tweet):

Negative sentiments all around. An unbalanced triad.

In a balanced platform, liberal accounts retweet liberal content and conservative accounts retweet conservative content, and each side disparages the other’s.
Balance at the triad level aggregates into echo chambers at the network level.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Adding New Nodes Preserves the Polarization Pattern
text:
Adding New Nodes Preserves the Polarization Pattern













Adding new nodes to the structure does not change the group polarization pattern, as long as their relationships to every other node are balanced.
I makes friends with C, D, and E.
H makes friends with A, B, and F.
Then they balance out the rest of the relationships with the other side.
Still polarized!

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Properties of Balanced Signed Graphs

Balanced signed graphs have some interesting properties. If a graph \(G\) is balanced:

Any subgraph of \(G\) is also balanced.
All paths between the same pair of nodes have the same sign as the link between them.
Cycles of any length are always positive (an even number of negative edges).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Sign of a Path













The sign of a path is the product of the signs of each edge in it.
\(F\) and \(I\) have a negative connection.
All paths connecting F and I are negative:

F–B–A–C–I: \((+1)(+1)(-1)(+1) = -1\)
F–B–E–I: \((+1)(-1)(+1) = -1\)

Positively connected nodes like E and C have all positive paths:

E–I–C: \((+1)(+1) = +1\)
E–D–C: \((+1)(+1) = +1\)

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Cycles Are Always Positive













In a balanced signed graph, cycles of any length are always positive.
3-cycle A–C–B: \((-1)(-1)(+1) = +1\)
5-cycle A–C–D–E–B: \((-1)(+1)(+1)(-1)(+1) = +1\)
Equivalent statement: every cycle contains an even number of negative edges.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Clustering Is a Weaker Criterion Than Balance
text:
Clustering Is a Weaker Criterion Than Balance

Balance demands two groups. But real signed networks often have more than two clusters.
Davis’s insight: clustering is a weaker criterion than balance.
A signed graph is clusterable when we can partition the nodes into clusters such that:

Positive links fall within clusters.
Negative links fall between clusters.

The all-negative triad — unbalanced under strict balance — is now allowed.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Building a Clusterable Network from Triads
text:
Building a Clusterable Network from Triads

Suppose we build a network whose triangles come in only three types:

All-positive triads (everybody inside a cluster likes everybody else in it).
Two-negative triads (two cluster-mates against an outsider).
All-negative triads (one node from each of three clusters).

Then we give the nodes names: \(\{a, d, e\}\), \(\{c, g\}\), and \(\{b, f, h\}\).
And now we connect them up!

Positives (\(+1\), green) sit inside each of the three clusters; negatives (\(-1\), red) sit between them.
Triads entirely within a cluster are all-positive; triads spanning two clusters have two negatives; triads spanning all three are all-negative.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Davis Shows That the Graph Has Three Clusters
text:
Davis Shows That the Graph Has Three Clusters













Davis shows that the nodes partition into three clusters:

Cluster 1: \(\{a, d, e\}\)
Cluster 2: \(\{c, g\}\)
Cluster 3: \(\{b, f, h\}\)

Positive links within clusters, negative links between them.
The all-negative triads (like \(\{a, b, c\}\), one node from each cluster) are what keep this from being strictly balanced — but it is perfectly clusterable.
